agency: North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), administered locally through 19 Human Service Zones
admin_note: North Dakota is STATE-SUPERVISED but delivered through a genuinely distinctive local structure: the 2019 Legislature's SB 2124 (North Dakota Century Code Chapter 50-01.1) dissolved the state's prior 47 county-run social service offices (across 53 counties) and re-formed them, effective January 1, 2020, into 19 mostly-multicounty "Human Service Zones," each hosted administratively by one lead county. This pack flags this Zone structure explicitly as a genuine structural departure from both a single-state-office model (like this roster's New Hampshire) and a plain county-administered model (like this roster's California, New York, Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Virginia) — North Dakota sits in between, with state supervision but zone-level delivery, and operative practice can still vary meaningfully by zone. GENUINE STRUCTURAL FLAGSHIP FINDING: North Dakota's SNAP policy manual was itself substantially RENUMBERED and re-platformed in 2025 — the legacy "430-05-xx-xx"-numbered manual (a stale mirror this pack found live at nd.gov/dhs/policymanuals/43005/, with several sections showing content dated a full year or more out of date, e.g. pre-OBBBA ABAWD criteria and a stale FFY2025 income table) has been superseded by a new plain-numbered manual ("100 Application" through "1200 EBT" plus an Appendix) at nd.gov/dhs/policymanuals/SNAP/, actively version-controlled with a public Release Log (Release 26.5 as of this pack's research, last published 06/15/2026) — this pack used ONLY the new, current manual's live content for every dollar figure and eligibility rule below, and flags the legacy 43005 mirror as a genuine staleness trap for any future research pass. SECOND FLAGSHIP FINDING, a genuine correction of a claim several secondary sources repeat with more confidence than a single source alone would justify: several SNAP-eligibility aggregator sites (povertylevelcalculator.com, snapbenefitshelp.com, and others this pack found) state North Dakota's SNAP resource/asset limit as $2,250 (all other households) / $3,250 (elderly or disabled households) — this pack fetched North Dakota HHS's own current SNAP manual section 601, Resources Overview (revised 5/16/2025), directly, and finds the CURRENT figures are $3,000 (all other households) and $4,500 (households with an elderly or disabled member) — matching the FFY2026 national baseline this roster's New Hampshire pack has also confirmed, not the lower $2,250/$3,250 figures the secondary sources repeat (which appear to be a much older, pre-COLA figure propagated without an update check). THIRD FLAGSHIP FINDING (primary-source confirmation of a minority-position claim): North Dakota fully opted out of the federal drug-felony SNAP ban via North Dakota Century Code § 50-06-05.1, effective 2017 — this pack cross-checked the statute's operative language directly ("the department may not deny assistance under the supplemental nutrition assistance program to any individual who has been convicted of a felony offense that has as an element the possession, use, or distribution of a controlled substance") against the current HHS SNAP manual's own disqualification sections (430-05-77-55 in the legacy manual), which list ONLY SNAP-trafficking-related disqualifications (sale of a controlled substance involving SNAP benefits, sale of firearms/ammunition/explosives involving SNAP benefits, fleeing felon/parole-violator status) and contain no general drug-felony-conviction ban at all — consistent with the statute. FOURTH FLAGSHIP FINDING, genuinely time-sensitive: North Dakota received a rare USDA SNAP demonstration-project waiver, approved by USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins on December 10, 2025, to exclude soft drinks, energy drinks, and candy from the SNAP-eligible food definition statewide, effective September 1, 2026 (a two-year pilot, extendable) — this pack fetched the USDA FNS approval letter directly and flags that, as of this pack's research date, this restriction is NOT YET IN EFFECT and applicants should be told the current effective date precisely rather than treated as already operative. FIFTH FINDING, directly relevant to this pack's tribal-land disclosure requirement: North Dakota's SNAP manual's own Vehicles section (604) states explicitly, "On Indian reservations that do not require vehicles driven by tribal members to be licensed, such vehicles must be treated as licensed vehicles" for resource-valuation purposes — a genuine, narrow, reservation-specific administrative rule this pack found stated in the state's own current manual text, distinct from the separate Food Distribution Program (Commodities/FDPIR) choice-of-program rules covered in the tribal-programs supplement. Confirm current operative practice with the applicant's own local Human Service Zone office, the same caution this roster already carries for its other built states.
system: North Dakota HHS administers SNAP through 19 Human Service Zones (state-supervised, zone-delivered, per North Dakota Century Code Chapter 50-01.1 and SB 2124, effective 1/1/2020). Applicants can apply online via the Self-Service Portal (dhsbenefits.dhs.nd.gov), by requesting a mailed application through an HHS online form, or in person/by mail using Application for Assistance form SFN 405 (available in English and Spanish) submitted to their local Human Service Zone office. The Customer Support Center assists with questions before and during the application process. North Dakota calls its program plainly "SNAP" — this pack found no distinctive state-specific brand name the way some states use (e.g., CalFresh, Basic Food). North Dakota tribal nations with reservation land operate the Food Distribution Program (FDPIR/Commodities) as a mutually-exclusive alternative to SNAP — an eligible household may choose either program but not both simultaneously, and may switch between them only at the end of a review/certification period (or upon voluntary termination and a new application). This pack found no evidence of a distinct SNAP administrative structure specific to the Turtle Mountain Reservation or North Dakota's other federally recognized tribal lands (Standing Rock, Spirit Lake, Fort Berthold/Three Affiliated Tribes, Sisseton-Wahpeton) beyond this Food Distribution Program choice-of-program framework and the reservation-specific vehicle-licensing rule in the resources/vehicles supplement — North Dakota's ABAWD policy separately carries a distinct "Indians, Urban Indians, or California Indians" (IHS-eligible) exemption category, covered in the abawd-work-requirement supplement.

verification.method: North Dakota HHS's own site (hhs.nd.gov) and the state's separate policy-manual host (nd.gov/dhs/policymanuals) both returned clean HTTP 200 to direct curl attempts with a standard browser User-Agent — no WAF barrier this pack encountered, distinct from several other states in this roster. The genuine access challenge this pack found was NOT a blocked-request barrier but a STALE-CONTENT trap: nd.gov/dhs/policymanuals/43005/ (the legacy numbered manual host, e.g. 430-05-xx-xx section citations) returned clean 200 responses with plausible-looking content, but that content was found to be up to a full COLA cycle (or, for ABAWD exemption criteria, a full year pre-OBBBA) out of date when cross-checked against the actively-maintained nd.gov/dhs/policymanuals/SNAP/ host's own public Release Log. This pack caught the trap by (1) noticing the legacy pages' income-limit dollar figures ($1,632 130% FPG for household size 1, revised '10/1/2024 ML 3858') did not match FFY2026-consistent secondary-source figures, (2) independently locating the new SNAP/ manual host via a Release Log entry, and (3) confirming via the Release Log's dated entries (25.6 effective 10/1/2025 for FFY2026 COLA figures; 25.7 effective 11/1/2025 for OBBBA ABAWD changes; 26.2 effective 4/1/2026 for a further SUA increase) that the new host's content was current and the legacy host's was not. This pack used ONLY the new SNAP/ manual host's content for every dollar figure and current-eligibility-rule claim below, and explicitly flags the legacy-host trap in freshness.json for any future research pass on North Dakota.
verification.gates: No WAF or bot-detection barrier was found on either hhs.nd.gov or nd.gov/dhs/policymanuals — both domains served clean HTTP 200 responses to a standard browser User-Agent on every attempt this pack made. The r.jina.ai reader proxy was used opportunistically (not out of necessity) to render several JavaScript-driven left-navigation pages on the new SNAP/ manual host so this pack could discover the current section URL structure; plain curl fetches worked for every individual content page and PDF once the correct URL was known. fns.usda.gov and fna.usda.gov (federal ABAWD waiver index and food-restriction-waiver approval letter) returned clean HTTP 200 to direct fetches with no barrier.
